LANDSCAPE AND VISUAL IMPACT
10.1.1.1 10.1.1.2 Introduction
The assessment of potential landscape and visual impacts due to construction and
operation of the Project is presented in this chapter.
Landscape and visual impacts were assessed in accordance with the criteria and
guidelines as stated in Section 1 of Annexes 10 and 18 of the Technical
Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Process (EIAO-TM) and the
latest version of Environmental Impact Assessment ordinance (EIAO) Guidance
Note No. 8/2023 on “Preparation of Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment
under the Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance”.
Scope and Content of the Study
Assessment Area
10.2.1.1 The assessment area for landscape impact assessment includes all areas within
100m from the boundary of the Project and its associated works in accordance with
EIA Study Brief (No. ESB-373/2025). The assessment area for the visual impact
assessment is defined by the visual envelope of the Project. The landscape and
visual impact study boundary are shown in Figure 10.1.0.
Landscape Impact Assessment
10.2.1.2 The existing and planned landscape resources and character within the
assessment area were described, appraised, analyzed and evaluated. A system is
derived for judging landscape and visual impact significance as required under the
Technical Memorandum. The sensitivity of the landscape framework and its ability
to accommodate change are particularly focused on. The degree of compatibility
of the Project with the existing and planned landscape setting was identified. The
landscape impact assessment evaluated the potential landscape impact so as to
illustrate the significance of such impacts arising from the proposed Project. Clear
mapping of the baseline landscape resources, landscape character areas and the
landscape impact were provided.
10.2.1.3 Visual Impact Assessment
The visual impact due to the Project during operation phase was assessed. For
aboveground roads and structures of the Project, clear illustrations including
mapping of visual impact are provided. The assessment adopts a systematic
methodology and includes the following.
(a) Identification and plotting of visual envelope of the Project;
(b) Appraisal of existing visual resources and character as well as the future outlook
of the visual system of the assessment area;
(c) Identification and justification of the key public viewing points within the visual
envelope and their views at sea level, ground level and elevated vantage points,
and clearly indicate the public viewing points on a plan of appropriate scale;
(d) Evaluation of the magnitude of change in terms of visual composition, visual
obstruction and visual change of the Project with the existing and planned visual
context, and sensitivity of viewers in terms of types of viewers and value of
existing views;

existing landscape and visual quality. Mitigation measures to minimise the adverse
effects identified, including provision of a landscape design, are recommended.

provision of finishes to structure, colour scheme and texture of material used, tree
compensation, provision of screen planting, roadside amenity planting, roof
greening and reprovision of open spaces.

section/elevation diagrams, oblique aerial photographs, photographs taken at key
public viewing vantage points and computer-generated photomontage are adopted
where appropriate to illustrate the significance of the landscape and visual impacts
of the aboveground roads and structures of the Project.

Landscape Impact Assessment Methodology
The landscape impact was assessed according to the following procedures:
• Carry out Broad Brush Tree/Vegetation Survey including distinctive
landscape resources within the Assessment Area. The survey would be
carried out within 100m from boundary of the Project and its associated works,
which is in accordance with the EIA Study Brief (No. 373/2025), to identify the
dominant tree species, maturity, rarity, and any plant species of conservation
importance, and the trees of particular interest (TPIs) as listed under Para.3 ,
Appendix I of the EIA Study Brief, etc. for the baseline study on the Landscape
Resources (LRs) and Landscape Character Areas (LCAs).” In case the tree
species listed in the Forestry Regulations (Cap 96A) under the Forests and
Countryside Ordinance (Cap. 96) are commercially cultivated, readily available
from nurseries and widely planted in Hong Kong’s urban landscape, these trees
will not be identified as trees of particular interest (TPI) in the Tree Schedule.
The broad brush tree (between 100m assessment area) and individual tree (in
accessible locations within the site boundary) survey findings including tree
survey plans, tree schedule and tree photographs are illustrated in Appendix i.
• All aboveground and underground construction activities including temporary
and permanent structures, are assessed in this report if they impose any
landscape impact within the assessment area. Only underground activities and
facilities unlikely to impose landscape impacts such as tunnelling, are not
assessed.
• Identification and description of the baseline LR and LCA found within the
Assessment area. The assessment area includes all areas within 100m from
boundary of the Project and its associated works. This is achieved by site visits and
desktop study of topographical maps, information databases and photographs.”
• Assessment of the degree of sensitivity of the LR and LCA. This is
influenced by a number of factors including whether the resource/character is
common or rare, whether it is considered to be of local, regional, national or
global importance, whether there are any statutory or regulatory
limitations/requirements relating to the resource, the quality of the
resource/character, the maturity of the resource and the ability of the
resource/character to accommodate change.
The sensitivity of each LR and LCA is classified as follows:
High: Medium: Important landscape resources and landscape character of
particularly distinctive in character or high importance, sensitive
to relatively small change.
Landscape resources and landscape character of moderately
valued landscape characteristics reasonably tolerant to change.
Low: Landscape resources and landscape character, the nature of
which is largely tolerant to change.
• Identification of potential sources of landscape impacts. These are the
various elements of the construction works and operation procedures that would
generate landscape impact.

Sources of Landscape Impact
The sources of landscape impact arising from the Project would create various
levels of landscape impact during construction and operational phases of the
Project. Potential impacts would result from the temporary and permanent works
during the construction phase and permanent aboveground roads and structure
elements during operational phase.
The NM Highway San Tin Section will be predominantly as aboveground structures
and minor underground structures, including the at-grade road / viaduct structures,
tunnels, tunnel portals, associated administration building, ancillary building and
portal plant building/ plant room, slope formation, and relevant road modification/
realignment of existing highway. The sources of temporary landscape impact were
expected from the following key aboveground construction works:
• Construction of associated administration building, ancillary building and portal
plant building/ plant room and tunnel portals for operation and maintenance;
• Construction works areas for site offices, stockpiling of construction;
• Modification of the existing landform to accommodate the development
proposals including the introduction of new embankments, cuttings, tunnel
portals and bridges;
• Demolition materials, storage of construction equipment and plant, etc; and
• Loss of existing trees and other vegetation due to the construction works.
The NM Highway San Tin Section constitutes the designated projects (DPs) in Part
I, Schedule 2 of EIAO (including items A.1, A.7, I.1, K.10 and Q.1).
• DP Item A.1: A carriage way for motor vehicles that is an expressway, truck
road, primary distributor or district distributor road
• DP Item A.7: A road tunnel or railway tunnel more than 800m in length between
portals
• DP Item I.1: A drainage channel or river training and diversion works located
less than 300m from the nearest boundary of an existing or planned
conservation area
• DP Item K.10: A depot for the storage of, or a manufacturing plant for the
manufacture of, explosives (as defined by section 2 of the Dangerous Goods
Ordinance (Cap. 295))
• DP Item Q.1: All projects involving earthworks, dredging works and other
building works partly or wholly in an existing or gazetted proposed country park
or special area, a conservation area, an existing or gazetted proposed marine
park or marine reserve, a site of cultural heritage, and a site of special scientific
interest.
The sources of landscape impact in the operational phase would include:
• Operation of the NM Highway San Tin Section, including the at-grade
road/viaduct, tunnel portal, associated administration building, ancillary building
and portal plant building/ plant room; and
• Permanent removal of existing trees and other vegetation.
